background_notes.fact: For finitely supported real sequences u,v, |sum_k u(k)v(k)| <= (sum_k u(k)^2)^(1/2)(sum_k v(k)^2)^(1/2). Thus a nonnegative sequence supported on a finite set E satisfies sum_E u <= |E|^(1/2)||u||_ell2. Reindexing by any bijection of Z, in particular k -> h-k for integer h, preserves the ell^2 norm.

background_notes.justification: For a finite common index set, (sum u^2)(sum v^2)-(sum uv)^2 = (1/2)sum_{i,j}(u_i v_j-u_j v_i)^2 >=0. Taking nonnegative square roots gives the inequality. Apply it with v=1_E for the shell ell^1 estimate. A bijection merely permutes the squared terms. The same finite-sequence inequality applies to shell norms in S002.

background_notes.fact: For t=2^(-1/2), 0<t<1 and sum_{r>=0}t^r=(1-t)^(-1); in particular every finite partial sum is bounded by (1-t)^(-1).

grounds.reason: The offset kernel is exactly 2^(-r/2)=t^r for nonnegative integer r, with nonnegative shell-norm factors.

background_notes.justification: Multiplying the finite partial sum through r=n by 1-t gives 1-t^(n+1), so it is bounded by (1-t)^(-1). Also t^n tends to zero: with a=1/t-1>0, (1+a)^n>=1+na, hence t^n<=1/(1+na). Taking the supremum of partial sums gives the stated sum. Together with the displayed per-offset Cauchy–Schwarz estimate this justifies the uniform kernel bound.

background_notes.justification: Every positive integer magnitude lies in exactly one such dyadic interval. For finite support the identity is a finite partition of the squared norm. Generally nonnegative sums are suprema over finite index sets; each finite set meets finitely many shells and finite subsums in shells are finite subsums of the full squared sequence, giving equality of the two suprema.

background_notes.fact: For a nonnegative family w on I={(a,b,c,d) in (Z\{0})^4:a+b+c+d=0}, put I_m={i in I:max(|a|,|b|,|c|,|d|)<=m}. Then sum_I w=sup_{m>=1}sum_{I_m}w. A subset sum is at most sum_I w, and restricting a sequence to |k|<=m cannot increase its ell^2 norm.

background_notes.justification: Define the sum of a nonnegative family as the supremum of its finite subsums. Each I_m is finite, and each finite subset of I is contained in an I_m by taking a maximum of finitely many coordinate magnitudes. These two observations identify the suprema without exchanging signed limits. Subset monotonicity follows by inclusion of finite subsums; norm monotonicity follows by deleting nonnegative squared terms. Thus the already proved uniform finite-support estimate passes to the full sum.
